title: Chapter 11 – Bloodless
html:
On the first morning of winter, Old Hu draws a knife across Lin Jian's forearm, and nothing happens.

It is not a dramatic test. They are in the granary, the forge banked low, frost on the inside of the single window. Old Hu simply takes the small skinning knife from the bench, the one he uses for leather, holds Lin Jian's arm out straight by the wrist, and draws the edge firmly across the inside of the forearm from elbow to wrist, the way a man would test a blade on a ham.

The skin dents. It goes white along the line of the edge, the way a drumhead goes white under a thumb. And then, when the knife has passed, it springs back, pink, unmarked.

Old Hu looks at the knife. He looks at the arm. He tests the edge of the knife on his own thumbnail, and shaves off a curl of nail as neatly as a carpenter's plane.

"Skin Tempering," he says.

Lin Jian looks at his arm. There is a faint coppery sheen to the skin, like the inside of a polished bowl, that was not there last month. It is gone if he turns his arm in the light.

"Took me three years," Old Hu says. "With a strong root pushing Qi into it every day." He sets the knife down on the bench, very carefully, and looks at the clay cup beside the tub, the bigger one he started leaving there a year ago, which Lin Jian fills every dawn with something the color of strong tea. "Eighteen months. A pseudo-root." He grunts. "Don't let anyone cut you in front of your cousins."

"I won't."

"And when you get to Flesh Forging," Old Hu says, "and you will, the way you're going, don't let anyone hit you in front of them either."

\ \ \*

The Qi follows the body, three weeks later.

The fourth layer comes on a night of hard frost, after the sixth of his weekly gold pills, with his mother sitting beside him on the floor. It is not a crack this time but a long, slow widening, like a river cutting its banks in a flood, and when it is over the channels in his back and legs are open and the space in his dantian is deep enough that he can feel the bottom of it only faintly, like a stone at the bottom of a well.

```
[Host Status Update]
Qi Refining: Layer 4
Host Qi Reserve: 4.02 / 5.60
Channels opened: back (8 / 8), legs (4 / 8)
Five-Gate Wheel efficiency: 27%
```

Lin Feng took three years to reach the fourth layer from the third. Lin Jian has taken ten months.

His mother looks at him for a long time in the cold light from the window.

"Fourth," she says.

He nods.

"In the courtyard," she says, "you're on your second."

"Yes, Mother."

She is quiet a moment longer. Then, unexpectedly: "Get your coat. And your boots."

\ \ \*

She takes him down to the frozen river below the terraces in the gray hour before sunrise, when no one is awake but the guards on the gate, who see Su Qinghe going out with her son and think nothing of it. The river is iced at the edges and running black and fast in the middle. Mist lies on it like smoke.

"You said you would teach me," he says. "When I had the fourth layer."

"I said we'd see what your five elements make of it." She stands on the bank with her hands in her sleeves. "Show me how you'd do it."

She shows him the seals first. Three of them: a gathering seal, a shaping seal, a releasing seal. The water element is drawn in, compressed, and thrown. She does it once, slowly, so he can watch, and a thread of water leaps from her two extended fingers across the river and cracks into a tree trunk on the far bank, twenty paces away, leaving a hole the size of his thumb.

He makes the seals. He feeds water into them, alone, the way he has learned to feed one element at a time. A thread of water dribbles from his fingertips and falls into the snow a pace in front of him.

His mother says nothing.

He tries again. And again. On the fifth try it reaches the river. On the twelfth, the far bank. And then he stops, and stands in the snow with his hands at his sides, and thinks.

She doesn't know it, but she has described a pressure jet.

The power of a jet is not in how much water it carries. It is in how narrow the throat is that it passes through. His mother's Tidal Spear comes out of her fingers as a thread the width of a knitting needle, because that is the width of the channel she shapes with the second seal. She has never made it narrower, because no one has ever told her that narrower would be better. Everyone in this world thinks of a spell's power as Qi, the way they think of a river's power as water. Nobody thinks about the nozzle.

He makes the gathering seal. He draws in water, and only water. Then, instead of making the shaping seal the way she does, with the two fingers spread a little apart, he presses them together until they touch, and feeds the water through the shaping in the smallest stream he can, like squeezing it through the eye of a needle. It is hard. The water fights him. It wants to spread.

He holds it. He releases.

There is a sound like a whip.

A thread of water no thicker than a horsehair leaps out of his fingers. He cannot see it. He can only see where it goes: across the river, through the mist, into the trunk of the tree on the far bank, just below his mother's hole. Bark flies.

They walk across the ice at the edge of the river and around by the stepping stones to look.

His mother's hole is the size of his thumb and as deep as the first joint of his finger. His is the size of a grain of rice. When she breaks a twig off and pushes it into his hole, it goes in up to her knuckles before it stops.

She stands there with the twig in the tree for a very long time.

"Needle," she says at last. "Not spear. Needle."

"It's harder to aim," he says. "And it doesn't hit as hard. It just goes deeper."

"It goes deeper," she repeats. She pulls out the twig and looks at it. "Where would you put a needle like that, Jian, if the thing in front of you was much stronger than you?"

He thinks about it. "Somewhere small," he says. "An eye. A joint. The hole in a shield."

His mother looks at him for a long moment. Then she nods, very slowly, and throws the twig in the river, and they walk home in silence.

```
[Host Spell Analysis: Tidal Spear Art (Yellow Rank) — Host Variant]
Channel throat: 1/14 standard
Penetration: ×4.3
Impact area: ×0.07
Note: Host has independently derived a nozzle optimization. Suggested designation: Needle.
```

\ \ \*

Old Pei vanishes in the first week of the snow.

He is a charcoal burner, a cheerful, gap-toothed mortal of sixty who lives with his son in a hut by the clamps in the oak woods below the eastern terraces, and he has supplied Old Hu with charcoal since the forge was built. He comes up the hill every tenth day with a cartload. On the tenth day after the first snow, he does not come.

Fourth Uncle's men find his axe leaning against the clamp, and his straw hat lying upside down in the snow a little way into the trees. No footprints, because it snowed again in the night. No blood.

Five days later, his son vanishes too.

The search party goes out the next morning. Father and Uncle Mao and Fourth Uncle, and three of the older cousins, Lin Bo and Lin Kai and Lin Dong, with Fourth Uncle's guards strung out behind them in a line with their mantle bracers lit and their swords drawn. Lin Jian is not allowed to go. Neither is his mother. She goes anyway, a quarter of an hour later, alone, and does not tell anyone.

Lin Jian sits on the eastern wall and watches the black line of searchers move slowly through the white trees below, and feels the cold in his hands, and waits.

They come back at dusk. Lin Bo is white as the snow. Lin Dong has been sick on his own boots.

They have not found Old Pei. They have found a wolf.

\ \ \*

It lies under a fallen cedar half a mile east of the clamps. A gray wolf, second rank, bigger than any wolf Lin Jian has ever seen, its fur thick with snow. There is nothing wrong with it that anyone can see. No wound. No blood.

That is the wrong thing, his mother says, when she tells it in the main hall that night, with the family gathered round the brazier. There is no blood. Not on the wolf. Not in it. The body is as light as a sack of straw, and the skin hangs loose on the bones like a coat on a hook, and on its throat, side by side, there are two small round burns the size of a thumbprint.

And around it, in a circle three paces wide, the snow is pink.

"Not red," she says. "Pink. Like someone breathed out blood into the air, and it fell as mist." She looks at the brazier. "I've seen that once before. In the islands. Fifteen years ago."

"What is it?" says Fourth Uncle.

"A blood refiner," says Su Qinghe. "A demonic cultivator. They draw the blood out of living things and burn it into Qi." She is quiet for a moment. "To drain a second-rank wolf without a fight, it would have to be at the ninth layer at least. Or more."

The brazier crackles.

"More," says Grandfather.

"Foundation Establishment," says Su Qinghe. "Possibly."

No one says anything for a long time.

Then Grandfather stands up. "From tomorrow," he says, "no one goes into the forest alone. Not to cut wood, not to check snares, not for anything. Groups of four, at the least, and one of them a cultivator at the fifth layer or above. Daylight only. No one goes past the stream line. The villagers sleep inside the walls when the snow is deep." He looks around the hall. "Wenhai. Write to the Sect. Tell them there is demonic activity on our border and we request help."

"Yes, Father," says Second Uncle.

Lin Jian, behind the screen, sees his hands. They are resting on his knees. They are perfectly still. Second Uncle's hands are never still.

\ \ \*

The Sect's reply comes in nine days. It is four lines long.

The Outer Affairs Hall thanks the Lin family for its report. Demonic activity has been reported in several valleys of the outer counties this winter. The Hall will investigate as its resources permit. The Hall reminds the Lin family that its delivery of two hundred talismans is due at the end of the season.

Grandfather reads it twice. Then he holds it over the brazier until it catches, and drops it, and watches it burn.

\ \ \*

"Blood refiners," says Old Hu that night, in the granary, "are the lowest of the demonic path."

He is sitting on the anvil block with a jar, as he so often is in the evenings now. But he is not drinking from it. He is turning it round and round in his one hand.

"Every demonic art takes something that isn't yours and makes it yours. Souls. Corpses. Luck. Blood is the easiest. Every living thing has it, and every living thing has Qi in it. A blood refiner draws it out, burns it, and the Qi goes into his own channels. Beast blood is weak. Mortal blood is better." He pauses. "A cultivator's blood is best. And a cultivator's blood with a strong root in it." He looks at the fire. "When they reach the Foundation, they can draw out the root with the blood. Take it into themselves. Keep it. So they hunt children. The ones with the strong roots. Two, three, four elements, very pure. They can smell them."

Lin Jian thinks of Lin Feng, with his blazing triple root. He thinks of himself, five dim lights on a black stele, and for the first time in his life he is glad of them.

"You've met one," he says.

Old Hu says nothing for a long time.

"There was one," he says at last, "who took my arm. With a blade that had soaked a hundred days in his own refined blood. That's what's in my shoulder, boy. A piece of him. Eating me." He sets the jar down untouched. "So, yes. I've met one."

Then he gets up and goes to the bed in the corner of the granary, and pulls out from under it the battered leather case that Lin Jian scanned a year ago, and opens it on the bench.

The etched iron spikes. The dark metal discs.

"Formation pins," says Old Hu. "And anchor plates." He lays them out in a row. "The pins hold a shape. The lines etched on them carry Qi from one to the next, like your father's ink carries it across his paper. The plates store a charge. Four pins in a square around a plate, and the right lines etched on them, and you get a binding. Six and you get a snare. Nine," he touches the ninth pin, "and you get a crushing pit. A charged nine-pin pit will hold a man at the Foundation for perhaps ten heartbeats. Not long. Long enough."

Lin Jian stares at them. "You told my mother you don't make weapons."

"I don't." Old Hu looks at him. "I never said anything about traps."

He picks up four of the pins and one plate and pushes them across the bench.

"Yours," he says. "Practice ones. Yellow grade, which is more than you deserve. Learn to set a four-pin binding. Learn to set it in the dark, in the snow, with your hands shaking. When you can do that, I'll show you the snare." He goes back to the anvil. "A blood refiner doesn't fight fair. So we don't let him fight at all. We make him charge a tree."

Lin Jian picks up a pin. It is cold and heavy and humming faintly under his fingers, like a bee in a bottle.

```

Note: Uneven etching depth at lines 3 and 6. Optimization possible.
```

He turns it over in his hands, and says nothing, and begins to learn.

\ \ \*

He sets the four-pin binding a hundred times that week. In the granary, by lamplight. On the threshing floor, in the snow, at dusk. Once, at Old Hu's insistence, blindfolded, with the old smith flicking pebbles at his ears. On the eighth night, Old Hu walks into the square of pins he has set on the granary floor, and stops dead, his foot held to the stones by four threads of dim red light, and grunts, and pulls it free with an effort that shows in his neck.

"Better," he says.

On the ninth morning, before dawn, Lin Feng finds him on the threshing floor setting the pins in the snow.

His brother is fourteen now, at the fifth layer, the tallest of all the cousins and the best spear in the family after Fourth Uncle. He stands at the edge of the threshing floor with his practice spear on his shoulder and watches for a while without saying anything. Then he says, "What are those?"

"Old Hu's."

"What do they do?"

Lin Jian steps back. "Walk across them."

Lin Feng looks at him suspiciously, and then shrugs and walks forward, and his foot comes down in the square, and stops. He pulls. It does not come. He pulls harder, and his face goes red, and Lin Jian sees the Qi of the fifth layer surge down his brother's leg and the red threads strain and part.

Lin Feng stands on the threshing floor with his mouth open.

"Four heartbeats," says Lin Jian. "With practice pins. Old Hu says a nine-pin pit holds a Foundation for ten."

Lin Feng looks down at the pins. Then at his brother.

"Teach me," he says.

So they practice together, in the dark before dawn, every morning for a week: Lin Feng's fire ring and Lin Jian's pins and Earthen Rampart and Cloudstep, one after another, trying combinations the way children try keys in a lock. A ridge to turn an attacker into the square. A vortex to push him into it. A ring of fire springing up around him the moment he is held. On the sixth morning they try it on Old Gou, who has volunteered with great enthusiasm and regrets it, and the farmer ends up sitting in a smoking circle of scorched snow with both feet pinned and his eyebrows singed, laughing so hard he cannot breathe.

"You two," he says, wiping his eyes. "You two are going to be trouble."

\ \ \*

On the seventh morning, they go a little too far.

It is not deliberate. They are only going down to the frozen river, inside the stream line, to try the pins on ice. But the river is mist and silence and black water, and when they reach the bank, Lin Jian stops so suddenly that Lin Feng walks into his back.

"What?"

Lin Jian does not answer. He is not sure what it is.

He has felt it before, at the edges of things. In the hall when Second Uncle smiles. On the ridge when the wolf pack passed. Not a pressure, like rank. Something else. A wrongness. The way a chord sounds when one string is out of tune.

It is coming from the far side of the river. From the trees on the far bank, under the mist. It is faint and cold and somehow wet, like a drop of water running down the inside of a collar, and it smells, in a way that has nothing to do with his nose, of iron and salt.

If you ever meet a man whose Qi smells of iron and salt, children, you run, and you do not stop running until you are home.

"We're going back," he says.

"We just got—"

"Feng. We're going back. Now. Don't run. Walk."

His brother looks at his face. Whatever he sees there, he does not argue. They walk back up through the terraces in the gray light, not hurrying, not looking back, and Lin Jian feels the cold wet wrongness at his back the whole way, until they reach the gate, and it fades.

At the top of the hill, Lin Feng stops and looks down at the river.

"There was something there," he says. It is not a question.

"I think so."

His brother looks at him a long moment. "How did you know?"

"I don't know," says Lin Jian, which is true. "I just felt it. Like when you know someone's looking at you."

Lin Feng says nothing for a while. Then he says, "We don't go down there again. Not until it's gone."

"No."

That afternoon, Lin Jian tells his grandfather that he thinks he smelled iron by the river, and the old man looks at him, and that night the guard on the gate is doubled.

\ \ \*

The storm comes at the end of the month.

It comes over the Beast Mountains from the northeast in the middle of the night: wind that howls through the courtyards like a living thing, and snow driven sideways, and the crack and slither of roof tiles giving way all over the hill. In the morning the household goes out into a world of white drifts and broken branches and finds that the library roof has lost a whole row of tiles over the back of the room.

Snow has come in through the gap and lain on the shelves all night, and the warmth of the hall below has melted it. Water has run down the walls. The bottom shelf, where Second Uncle keeps ten years of account books, is a sodden ruin of swollen paper and running ink. The second shelf is not much better.

And the lacquered tube with the brass cap, the one that holds Lin Shoucheng's land deed, the one Grandfather has been looking at every night for a month while he searched for a second copy, is not there.

They search for it all day. They take every book and scroll off every shelf. They search the floor and the drifts outside and the gutters. It is not there.

Grandfather stands in the middle of the wrecked library at dusk with a lamp in his hand and his face like gray stone. Second Uncle stands beside him saying how terrible it is, how unlucky, the worst storm in years. His voice is warm and sorrowful. His hands are still.

Lin Jian climbs up onto the library roof that evening, while the others are at dinner, and looks at the gap where the tiles came away.

Most of the broken tiles lie in the drift below the eaves. One of them has caught on the edge of the gutter. He picks it up and turns it over in his hands, and sees, on the edge of it, a fresh bright scrape in the old glaze. And another. Two parallel scratches, the width of a blade, where something flat and hard was pushed under the tile and levered upward.

He lays his palm on the scratches and scans.

```
[Scan: Roof Tile (Damaged)]
Fracture: tensile, initiated at lower edge
Surface marks: 2 parallel gouges, 4 mm apart, depth 0.6 mm
Residue in gouges: steel (low carbon), trace brass
Note: Marks consistent with prying by a flat steel tool, not wind loading.
```

A pry bar. Or a knife. Or the flat steel edge of the kind of silver pencil case a man keeps in his sleeve, with a brass cap on the end.

It is not proof. A scratch on a tile is not proof. He knows exactly what Lin law says about proof.

But he sits on the roof in the dark for a long time anyway, holding the tile, looking down through the gap in the roof at the wrecked shelf where the deed used to be.

Because there is one thing on this hill that Second Uncle does not know about, and it is not a second copy.

Five years ago, when he was a small boy learning to climb the library shelves, Lin Jian put his hand on a lacquered tube with a brass cap, the way he put his hand on everything in those days, and let the blue line sweep. He was looking for Creation Energy. He did not even read what was inside.

He opens the library in his head now and finds it, exactly where it has always been.

```
[Blueprint: Land Deed (Lin Shoucheng)]
Material: aged hemp paper, pine-soot ink, vermilion seal paste
Estimated age: 140–160 years
Ink and seal deposition pattern: CAPTURED (full surface map)
Fabrication: Level 2 required
```

Full surface map. Every fiber of the paper. Every grain of ink in every stroke of every character. Every speck of vermilion in the magistrate's seal.

Lin Jian sits on the roof in the dark with the snow coming down around him, and looks at the blueprint, and does not move for a very long time.
